title: Decoding mitochondrial proteomes of diverse eukaryotes.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: This paper is a 3-page paywalled overview (Cell 189:6243-6245) with no full text, so I used the MitoCarta Tree of Life consortium data it introduces. I downloaded all six per-organism xlsx files from mitocarta.org (Acanthamoeba 15,944 genes / 1,122 mitochondrial; Arabidopsis 27,559 / 1,609; Babesia 4,132 / 525; Giardia 4,968 / 59; Leishmania 8,470 / 1,594; Trypanosoma 9,678 / 1,666). That is 70,751 genes and 6,575 positives, with no duplicate gene IDs. Each file has a 'Descriptions' sheet documenting every column, a continuous 'PCP score' (correlation of mass-spec profiles with mitochondrial marker proteins), a binary MitoCarta label, an evidence column, and DeepLoc2.1/TargetP2.0 prediction columns. I also opened mitotol_mitoproteomes.v2.xlsx (167,812 rows of predicted plus experimental mitoproteomes for 206 species), counted rows in mitotol_whole_proteomes.csv (3,437,290 rows: protein ID and predicted score only, no sequences), listed the Zenodo record files (CC-BY-4.0; species_fastas 3.2 GB, data.tar.xz 3.8 GB) and read the GitHub deeploc README.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Everything about this overview itself comes from the abstract alone. The fact that the companion paper (Chen et al., Cell 2026, 10.1016/j.cell.2026.08.029) retrained a protein-language-model classifier on these mitoproteomes comes from its abstract and the GitHub README, which mentions a GraphPart homology-partitioned weights folder. I did not see that classifier's performance numbers or whether it was tested leave-one-species-out. Sequences were not opened: the 3.2 GB species_fastas archive is over the size cap.

a1_downloadable.note: All six xlsx files downloaded without a login from mitocarta.org (checked). The Zenodo record is open, CC-BY-4.0.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The binary label (AcMitoCarta, AtMitoCarta, ... columns) and the continuous PCP score are ready-made columns in each 'All genes' sheet (checked). Nothing needs to be constructed.

a3_inputs_present.note: There are no sequences in the xlsx, only gene IDs (VEuPathDB, TAIR, GenBank). They resolve by one bulk proteome FASTA per organism (or Zenodo species_fastas, 3.2 GB), not thousands of lookups. This is a minor step, not a killer.

a4_units_stated.note: Labels are binary 0/1. The PCP score is a Pearson correlation from -1 to 1, with -1 meaning not detected, as documented in the Descriptions sheet (checked).

a5_enough_rows.note: 70,751 labelled genes across 6 organisms, 6,575 of them positive (counted). Giardia has only 59 positives.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~53 MB xlsx plus ~100 MB of proteome FASTA; 70k ESM-2 embeddings is about 0.1-0.3 GB
a6_fits_laptop.note: Tabular data. Embedding 70k proteins with a small ESM-2 (protein language model) on CPU takes hours, not days.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: My 6,575 positives plus human MitoCarta3.0 (1,136) and yeast come to about 8,600, which matches the companion abstract's 8,619 distinct mitochondrial proteins across eight organisms. The per-species experimental sizes in mitotol_mitoproteomes match, e.g. Trypanosoma 1,666 in both.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels come from measurement: mass-spec protein correlation profiling, microscopy, or being encoded in the mitochondrial genome. The DeepLoc/TargetP columns and the 198 predicted mitoproteomes are model outputs and must be excluded as labels or features. The 'BenchmarkLabel' column is derived from homology, so it is not a measured label.

B1.why: Six per-organism xlsx tables with a gene ID key; they need concatenating plus a join to proteome FASTA (checked).

B2.why: xlsx parsed first try with pandas, but column names differ per organism and need mapping (checked).

B3.why: Same mass-spec workflow throughout, but PCP sample sets differ by organism; Arabidopsis has five PCP score variants (checked).

B4.why: PCP score of -1 means 'not detected', a censored value; undetected genes are labelled 0 rather than truly negative (checked).

B5.why: 0 duplicate gene IDs in each 'All genes' sheet (checked).

B6.why: Every file has a Descriptions sheet defining each column (checked for Acanthamoeba, others have the same sheet).

C1.why: A leave-one-lineage-out transfer curve is informative whichever way it comes out: shows how predictors decay with evolutionary distance.

C2.why: The authors retrained DeepLoc2.0 (DeepLoc2.0-mito) on these data with a homology split. TargetP2.0, MitoFates and DeepLoc2.1 also exist.

C3.why: Weak 'better/diversity' angle: an honest held-out-lineage evaluation and a continuous PCP score target, unless the authors already did it.

C4.why: Each experimental mitoproteome took a multi-lab consortium years of organelle mass spectrometry.

C5.why: DeepLoc2.1 and TargetP2.0 predictions are already columns in the files: ready-made baselines (checked).

D1.why: ESM-2 (protein language model) has open weights; ProtT5 too.

D2.why: Cache mean-pooled plus N-terminal ESM-2 embeddings once on CPU; logistic head.

D3.why: Data are CC-BY-4.0 on Zenodo, ESM-2 is MIT; the DeepLoc2.0 base needs a DTU academic licence, but only for the baseline.

E1.why: Leave-one-organism-out across 6 lineages, plus a homology-cluster split.

E2.why: 6 organisms plus human and yeast MitoCarta = 8 groups; Giardia is small (59 positives).

E3.why: Majority class and a TargetP/DeepLoc-column threshold are computable from the files.

E4.why: Babesia has two PCP score replicate columns; Arabidopsis has several PCP subsets (checked).

E5.why: Orthologs of human MitoCarta3.0 proteins (column present) and N-terminal targeting signals should be recovered.

E6.why: Label shuffling, and N-terminus-only vs whole-protein feature ablation.

E7.why: Human MitoCarta3.0 and yeast mitoproteomes are independent experimental sets from other labs and methods.

E8.why: The DeepLoc2.0-mito performance numbers are in a paywalled paper I couldn't read.

G1.why: TAIR, VEuPathDB and GenBank gene IDs plus taxonomy IDs; UniProt top-hit columns present (checked).

G2.why: Human MitoCarta3.0 and UniProt subcellular location, joinable via UniProt/ortholog columns.

G3.why: Ortholog joins are one-to-many (gene families); proteome FASTA has isoforms (e.g. AT1G01010.1).

G4.why: Question: does mitochondrial targeting learned in animals and fungi transfer to deep-branching protists? Partly addressed by the authors.

H1.why: The whole proteome is listed with 0/1 labels; negatives cover every non-mitochondrial gene (checked).

H2.why: Six lineages: plant, amoeba, kinetoplastids, apicomplexan, diplomonad, all from one consortium.

H3.why: Claim is precise: mass-spec-detectable mitochondrial residency in standard lab growth conditions.

H4.why: Undetected low-abundance proteins labelled 0; only partly obvious from the -1 PCP score convention.

I1.why: Mootha/Calvo MitoCarta group; parasitologists annotating non-model protist proteomes.

I2.why: Would tell them which predictor to trust for new lineages; doesn't redirect experiments by itself.

I3.why: The decision is binary (in mitoproteome or not); PR-AUC (precision-recall area under the curve) matches it.

I4.why: Ortholog lookup to human MitoCarta likely solves much of it; ML adds value for lineage-specific proteins.

J1.why: Embeddings, grouped CV (cross-validation), transfer across lineages, calibration.

J2.why: Mitochondrial targeting biology is intuitive, but protist-specific proteins are hard to sanity-check.

J3.why: A benchmark of TargetP/DeepLoc per lineage is shareable before any model is trained.

existing_models.name: DeepLoc2.0-mito (Chen et al., Cell 2026; github michaelzhuchen/mito-evolution)
existing_models.score_and_split: Retrained on these experimental mitoproteomes with a GraphPart homology-partitioned split (folder name in README); scores not seen (paywalled).

existing_models.name: DeepLoc 2.1 (subcellular localization predictor)
existing_models.score_and_split: Its predictions are already columns in every file; its published scores not retrieved.

existing_models.name: TargetP 2.0 (targeting-peptide predictor)
existing_models.score_and_split: Its predictions are already columns in the files; published scores not retrieved.

existing_models.name: DeepMito (sub-mitochondrial localization CNN)
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on 424 proteins with experimental sub-mitochondrial evidence; a different task (compartment within mitochondria).

backbone.name: ESM-2 (protein language model; 35M or 150M checkpoint)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU; ~70k proteins embedded in a few hours

integration.partner_dataset: Human MitoCarta3.0 plus yeast mitoproteome (already referenced via Human.TopHit and Yeast.TopHit columns); UniProt subcellular location
integration.join_key: Gene ID to UniProt top-hit / ortholog columns
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: How far from animals and fungi can sequence-based mitochondrial targeting rules be trusted, and which lineages break them?

controls.positive_control: Proteins orthologous to human MitoCarta3.0 entries and those with strong N-terminal targeting signals should score highest; sequence length as a trivial target.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffle within organism; N-terminal-region-only vs full-sequence ablation.
controls.external_validation: Train on the six MitoTOL organisms, test on human MitoCarta3.0 and yeast (independent experiments), or hold out one lineage at a time.

honest_claim_h3: Predicts whether a protein is detected as mitochondrial by organelle mass spectrometry under standard lab growth, across six lineages from one consortium; low-abundance or condition-specific mitochondrial proteins are silently labelled negative.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a protein's amino-acid sequence to predict whether it lives in the mitochondrion, testing on lineages the model never saw.
plain_idea.train_on: Protein sequences from six distantly related organisms (a plant, an amoeba and four parasites): 70,751 genes, 6,575 of them experimentally mitochondrial (counted).
plain_idea.predict: Whether the protein belongs to the organism's mitochondrial inventory, as measured by mass-spec co-fractionation with known mitochondrial markers (plus microscopy), or the continuous correlation score itself.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Parasitologists annotating new protist genomes would learn how much to trust predicted mitoproteomes as distance from the training lineages grows.

more_or_better_data.why: The authors' own DeepLoc2.0-mito was retrained on exactly these experimental mitoproteomes, so we have no more data than they did.

confidence_score.why: The continuous PCP score and Babesia's replicate PCP columns could support per-protein uncertainty; I didn't verify whether DeepLoc2.0-mito reports calibration.

models_beatable.why: DeepLoc2.0-mito is 2026, built on ProtT5 (protein language model) with a homology split, so it is hard to beat. TargetP2.0 (2019) and DeepLoc2.1 are older baselines trained mostly on animals, fungi and plants.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No accessible new data measures the same quantity the same way beyond what DeepLoc2.0-mito already saw; the human and yeast sets were likely in its training.

label_elsewhere.sources: Human MitoCarta3.0 and yeast mitoproteomes (known resources, referenced in the files); UniProt subcellular location annotations (known resource); Human Protein Atlas subcellular atlas (known resource).
label_elsewhere.why: Annotated mitochondrial localization across many species allows external tests and pretraining beyond these six organisms, though most of it is annotation, not uniform measurement.

ambitious.why: Publishes careful benchmarks with biological insight; it would need a clear decay-with-distance curve plus lineage-specific failure modes.

realistic.why: A per-lineage benchmark of mitochondrial localization predictors on new experimental ground truth fits its benchmark track.

fallback.journal: bioRxiv preprint plus NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics
fallback.why: Even a 'predictors fail on Giardia and Babesia' result is a publishable negative benchmark.

pitch.headline: 70,751 proteins from six deep-branching eukaryotes, each with an experimental mitochondrial label: rare ground truth outside animals, fungi and plants.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Whole-proteome negatives and positives (6,575) measured by one mass-spec workflow in amoeba, kinetoplastids, Babesia and Giardia, CC-BY-4.0, with every column documented (checked).
pitch.the_win: A leave-one-lineage-out curve showing TargetP2.0/DeepLoc2.1 PR-AUC dropping with evolutionary distance, and a frozen ESM-2 head recovering part of the gap on held-out lineages.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: A per-lineage benchmark of existing predictors against experimental mitoproteomes, which tells annotators where those predictions are unreliable.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Mootha/Calvo MitoCarta group and VEuPathDB parasite-genome annotators deciding whether to trust predicted mitoproteomes for unstudied protists.

ml_idea: Embed the 70,751 proteins with frozen ESM-2, fit a logistic head, evaluate leave-one-organism-out against the DeepLoc2.1/TargetP2.0 columns already in the files, and test on human/yeast MitoCarta; secondary task: regress the continuous PCP score.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: ~70k sequences of median ~400 residues at ~5 proteins/s with ESM-2 35M on CPU; a logistic head on 480-dimensional embeddings takes minutes.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the Chen et al. 2026 methods (via a library or the Zenodo README) to see whether they already report leave-one-species-out DeepLoc2.0-mito performance. If they do, the novelty is gone.

verdict_reason: The data are excellent and checked: 70,751 measured labels, documented, open. But the authors already retrained a protein-language-model classifier on them with a homology split. First confirm they did not publish leave-one-lineage-out results; only that transfer benchmark remains as an angle.
